metadata.title: Motivation towards mathematics from 1980 to 2015: Exploring the feasibility of trend scaling

survey_design.weight_variable_name: senate weights (rescaled; SIMS stratum weights rescaled to senate weights)
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study pooled grade 8 (or equivalent) student questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS cycles 1995–2015 for seven ILSAs, but restricted the analytic systems to England, Hong Kong, Hungary, Israel, Japan, and the United States (with Japan excluded from latent-variable analyses after poor measurement invariance). To account for unequal sample sizes across countries and for TIMSS 1995 having two sampled adjacent grades in each country (except Israel), the authors applied senate weights that sum to 500 for each country’s data. In SIMS, stratum weights were rescaled to senate weights, and within-country grade weighting was adjusted so each grade contributed equally. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it notes that standard errors of means may be underestimated because the simple random sampling assumption does not fully match TIMSS’s stratified multistage design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes; instead, it constructs and compares trend scales for affective motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) using CFA/IRT-based scaling and a market-basket approach. Because the dependent variables are affective scale scores derived from measurement models and plausible-response generation (not PVs for cognitive achievement), PV handling is not applicable. Missing responses are handled via full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) and a market-basket procedure that imputes missing responses five times per respondent to generate plausible scores, so missing-data handling is reported as multiple imputation rather than PV combining.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study pooled grade 8 (or equivalent) student questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS cycles 1995, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011, and 2015, but selected only the six educational systems that participated in all time points: England, Hong Kong, Hungary, Israel, Japan, and the United States. For the latent-variable (CFA/MGCFA) comparability analyses, Japan was excluded after measurement invariance did not hold (negative factor loadings in baseline models). For the questionnaire response processing, the authors did not treat the SIMS middle response option as missing due to its large proportion; instead, they recoded middle responses to random answers between agree and disagree. Students who selected the middle option for all items were excluded (0.95% for extrinsic and 0.71% for intrinsic). Missing responses within the motivation items were retained and handled through FIML in Mplus for the CFA/IRT scaling steps and through a market-basket plausible-response generation procedure (five imputations per respondent) for the market-basket scaling.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper investigates how to construct comparable trend scales for two affective mathematics motivation constructs (intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) across decades using grade 8 (or equivalent) questionnaire data from SIMS 1980 and TIMSS cycles 1995–2015. The analytic systems were England (GBR), Hong Kong (HKG), Hungary (HUN), Israel (ISR), Japan (JPN), and the United States (USA), with Japan excluded from latent-variable analyses after cross-cultural measurement invariance did not hold. The authors compare three scaling approaches: (1) CFA-based scaling with MGCFA invariance testing, (2) IRT-based scaling using PCM vs GPCM (GPCM selected for better fit), and (3) a market-basket approach that generates plausible responses five times per respondent using country-specific measurement models and then computes standardized sum scores. Across methods, correlations between individual scores were very high (0.96 to 1.00), and country-level trends from CFA/IRT under invariance assumptions closely matched observed scores. A key limitation is that standard errors of means may be underestimated because TIMSS’s stratified multistage sampling design is not fully reflected when standard errors are computed under simple random sampling assumptions. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a scaling/methodology study focused on measurement invariance and trend construction for affective motivation scales rather than an empirical machine-learning prediction study. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, no PV-based cognitive achievement targets, and no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE/AUC) to extract into main_findings. The paper’s core outputs are psychometric/measurement results (invariance testing, scaling correlations, and trend comparisons), so the ML-specific fields are intentionally empty.
